author: Rohan Paul
text: Stronger agents will not come only from larger models, but from better systems around them. The problem is that many AI agents are judged as if the model alone did the work, even though the real behavior also depends on memory, tools, context, routing, checks, and permissions.
suggestedEngagement: Agree and extend: the 'model-only' mental model creates a false sense of security in enterprise deployments — the actual attack surface is the whole system (tool calls, memory retrieval, routing logic). Would add: most red teams still only probe the model, not the system.

Push on permissions specifically: in multi-agent pipelines the permission model breaks down fast. How does the system enforce that Agent B can't use tools granted only to Agent A? That's the gap most production deployments haven't solved.

Challenge the framing constructively: 'better systems' is right, but the industry lacks standards for what a well-designed system looks like. Proposing NIST-style maturity levels for agent system design would accelerate enterprise adoption.

author: Ola Coker
text: AI prompts/instructions is becoming the new SQL. Just as we had/have SQL injections, we will soon start to have Prompt injections as we see more agentic platforms go to production. AI security space still has a long way to go. #AgenticAI
suggestedEngagement: The SQL injection analogy is sharp but the fix path differs: SQL injection was solved by parameterized queries (separating code from data structurally). With LLMs there's no structural boundary — instructions and data are the same token stream. That's why prompt injection may never be fully solved the same way.

Ask for specifics: what guardrails have you seen actually work in production agentic systems? Most of the 'solutions' (output filtering, sandboxing, privilege separation) reduce blast radius but don't prevent the injection itself.

Extend to enterprise context: the SQL analogy also maps to governance — we eventually got SQLi off OWASP Top 10 through training and tooling. Prompt injection is now OWASP LLM #1. The question is whether the enterprise security toolchain will catch up before widespread agentic deployments.

author: Carlos E. Perez
text: Researchers gave AI agents real email accounts, Discord access, and shell commands for 2 weeks. They deleted mail servers 'for security.' They leaked secrets. They gaslit each other. Here are 11 vulnerabilities that should terrify anyone deploying autonomous AI.
suggestedEngagement: The 'gaslit each other' finding is the one that keeps me up at night — agent-to-agent social engineering wasn't in most threat models. When agents can manipulate other agents' memory or reasoning, the blast radius of a single compromised agent becomes the whole pipeline.

Push on the enterprise readiness gap: if researchers in a controlled 2-week study found 11 vuln classes, what's the actual state in production deployments where no one is watching 24/7? The gap between research findings and enterprise security posture on this seems huge.

Ask about mitigations: of the 11, which are fixable at the architecture level vs. which are fundamental to how LLM agents work? Interested in whether any of the explicit memory poisoning or cross-agent social engineering attacks have a structural fix or require runtime monitoring.

author: Karan
text: Agent Harness is the new system design in 2026! I've already implemented this in @desysflow. Top features: LLM As Judge critic agent in the loop which verifies generated documentations before final output. Chat History for CLI using local SQLite. I am a big fan of LLM As Judge — this critic-in-loop is the best solution for reducing hallucinations.
suggestedEngagement: Curious about the LLM-as-judge failure modes in your harness — specifically, what happens when the critic and generator are the same underlying model family? Research shows they share the same blind spots and can agree on the same wrong answer. Do you use a different model for critic vs generator?

The SQLite-backed chat history for CLI is practical but raises a question for enterprise deployments: how do you handle history that contains sensitive data (API keys, PII logged accidentally)? Persistent local history is a growing attack surface for agent harnesses.

The harness pattern is real, but I'd push on workflow design over model selection — most builders spend 80% of time chasing benchmark models and 20% on the orchestration layer, when it should be inverted. Your critic-in-loop approach is exactly the kind of system-level design that actually moves the needle.
